description: I'm Edward Guillen Morejon, Founder & CEO of ANAIS Technology LLC and Aegis Air Intelligence Systems LLC. My interests include aerospace engineering, AI, lunar exploration, digital twins, and intelligent systems. Our team aims to develop innovative solutions for lunar missions through scientific computing and collaboration. We're seeking developers, aerospace enthusiasts, data scientists, UI/UX designers, and researchers passionate about advancing space exploration.
summary:
Executive summary
ANAIS LunarLink™ — A Lunar Landing Odyssey is a proposed intelligent lunar mission-support environment developed as a NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 project. The concept combines landing-site exploration, mission visualization, navigation-oriented reasoning and human-centered decision support in a single accessible interface. Its purpose is to help students, engineers, researchers and mission planners explore how candidate landing areas could be compared transparently before increasingly sophisticated mission simulations are attempted. The project is an independent competition entry and is not an official NASA mission, NASA-endorsed product or flight-qualified system.
details:
The problem we are addressing

A lunar landing is a systems problem rather than an isolated descent maneuver. Terrain slope, craters, illumination, communications line of sight, surface hazards, available energy and uncertainty can all influence mission decisions. A site that seems promising in a simple image may be unacceptable after a second constraint is considered. Even in an educational simulation, these considerations are difficult to communicate when information is scattered among static maps, calculations and narrative descriptions. We propose a coherent interface that makes assumptions visible and allows candidate sites to be explored rather than presenting an unexplained “best site.”

Our proposed solution

LunarLink is organized around a landing-site analysis workflow: identify a candidate region, review relevant terrain and mission constraints, calculate or display comparative indicators, inspect trade-offs, and document the resulting advisory rationale. ANAIS™ serves as the research-oriented intelligence layer. In the intended architecture, it would organize data provenance, flag missing inputs, communicate uncertainty, and explain why a site appears favorable or unfavorable. The ultimate authority for mission operations would remain with qualified human operators and independently validated flight systems.

What the current prototype demonstrates

The project’s packaged web prototype has been described in recent development records as including a landing animation and an interactive landing-site analyzer using synthetic scenario inputs. These artifacts demonstrate user interaction, a possible scoring workflow and mission storytelling—not validated lunar geospatial predictions. Earlier package checks reportedly passed seven scoring-related tests along with JavaScript syntax, asset reference and navigation checks. Those checks do not establish correctness against NASA scientific data. At the time of this document, live public deployment, full browser acceptance testing and integration of an operational LunarNav scientific engine have not been independently confirmed. Judges should review the repository and demonstrations directly for the latest actual state.

A lunar landing odyssey: end-to-end mission vision

The broader mission narrative follows five linked phases. Odyssey represents the transport and mission-coordination segment; lunar orbit provides the staging and situational-awareness context; Atlas represents a conceptual descent and landing vehicle; Pathfinder represents surface mobility and local inspection; and Haven represents a prospective surface habitat and longer-duration operations node. This sequence gives judges a way to see how a landing-site decision connects to subsequent exploration, supplies, surface safety and communications. These named vehicles and facilities are conceptual elements of a proposed ANAIS and VELORA ecosystem; they are not presented as built spacecraft or validated operational hardware.

Technical architecture and responsible AI

The architecture separates the presentation layer, scenario-input layer, analysis logic and future data-integration services. The front end should let a user inspect input values, compare candidates and see which weights or constraints affect an evaluation. A research-grade progression would replace synthetic values with traceable lunar data, record dataset versions and coordinate systems, implement deterministic reference calculations, and measure outputs against published baselines. AI-supported interpretation may assist comprehension, but scientific inputs, numerical analysis and human approval must remain auditable. This separation is especially important in aerospace work, where a persuasive visualization must never be mistaken for engineering validation.

Expected value and use cases

Near-term value comes from education, communication and rapid prototyping. Instructors can demonstrate why landing-site selection involves trade-offs; student teams can test alternative scoring assumptions; researchers can discuss dataset limitations; and a public showcase can make lunar exploration more approachable. Longer-term research opportunities include polar illumination assessments, terrain traversability, orbital-to-surface communications visibility, mission digital twins, robotic mission coordination and resource prospecting. These extensions require substantial data acquisition, testing and expert validation before they can support operational claims.

Validation and delivery roadmap

The first milestone is to publish a working, reproducible demonstration with a readable README, screenshots, usage instructions, clear synthetic-data labeling, known limitations and an accessible source repository. The second milestone is to connect documented lunar datasets and establish baseline comparisons for landing-site calculations. The third is to introduce scenario-based tests, sensitivity analysis and uncertainty display, including failures for absent or incompatible inputs. Future research can add mission-communications constraints, digital-twin state tracking and multi-agent operations simulations. Each new capability should be distinguished as proposed, implemented, tested or externally validated.

Repository for judges

GitHub: https://github.com/remyvelora12-coder/anais-lunarnav

The repository was previously described as private. It must be made public or access must be explicitly granted to judges before submission. The proposed GitHub Pages address has not been verified live and is therefore not used as evidence of deployment.

Conclusion

ANAIS LunarLink™ aims to turn a complex aerospace question into an inspectable learning and research experience: how might a team compare possible lunar landing sites while communicating the reasons and uncertainties behind each decision? The current demonstration is a foundation rather than a finished flight system. Its contribution is the integrated workflow, transparent educational approach and extensible roadmap linking landing analysis to a larger lunar mission architecture. The project invites evaluation of what is implemented today, alongside a technically grounded path toward more rigorous scientific integration.
